strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem—annotation-free 6D pose estimation and tracking from a single 3D model—and delivers a complete, working system (segmentation, pose estimation, failure detection, and re-registration) rather than an isolated component.

The segmentation module (SOM) achieves strong results on the standard BOP benchmark suite (Table 2: 68.5 mean mAP across five datasets), outperforming unsupervised baselines such as CNOS and SAM6D on most datasets, with competitive runtime (0.183s), and it even surpasses a supervised baseline on average.

The reformulation of tracking-failure detection as a binary classification task with a lightweight attention-based verifier (TOM) is a sensible, well-motivated idea, and the ablation in Table 4 (cosine similarity 87.55% vs. 98.36% with one attention layer, at only ~1ms overhead) cleanly supports the design choice.

End-to-end pose results (Table 1) show that STORM approaches the ground-truth-mask upper bound on YCB-Video and closes most of the gap on LM-O, convincingly demonstrating that the segmentation module is the bottleneck being fixed.
The authors contribute a new tracking dataset and open-source plans, and the ablation studies (language injection, HSFA depth, DINOv2 fine-tuning) show genuine effort to validate design decisions.
weaknesses: The central 'no manual annotation / self-supervised' framing is overstated: SOM is trained on ground-truth masks from BOP training sets (Appendix C/D explicitly state 'each query image and its corresponding mask are subjected to joint photometric and geometric transforms'), and TOM training also uses ground-truth masks from BOP. Compared to truly training-free baselines like CNOS, this is a weaker supervision setting, so the 'Self-Supervised' category in Table 2 and the label-free claims need much more careful qualification.

There are material internal inconsistencies between the main text and the appendix that undermine reproducibility: the main paper reports a Tversky+Focal loss with alpha=0.3, beta=0.7, lambda_T=1.0, lambda_f=0.2 and AdamW, while Appendix D lists Tversky alpha=0.5, beta=0.5, w_Tversky=0.2, w_Focal=20.0 plus Dice and IoU losses, and SGD optimization. These cannot both be correct.

The 'real-time' claim is marginal: 0.183s/image (~5.5 FPS), rising to 0.265s with language injection; this should be presented more honestly, and end-to-end system FPS (SOM + FoundationPose + TOM) is not reported.

The end-to-end pose evaluation (Table 1) is thin: only two baselines (a DINO+SAM2 pipeline and the GT-mask upper bound) on two datasets; strong model-based methods such as SAM-6D, Megapose, or GigaPose in the same annotation-free regime are not compared, and no variance or significance is reported.

The tracking-failure evaluation relies on synthetic modifications (random frame dropping and randomly masking object regions on YCB-Video), which are crude proxies for real occlusion and rapid motion; no comparison to existing re-detection/recovery strategies (e.g., Siam R-CNN re-detection) is provided, only 'FP Tracking' without failure detection.

Methodological novelty is modest: the pipeline assembles established components (DINOv2, CLIP, AdaNormZero-style conditioning, SAM2/FastSAM, FoundationPose), and HSFA is essentially standard cross-attention between query and multi-view reference embeddings; the paper would benefit from a clearer articulation of what is genuinely new versus engineered.

Several presentation issues reduce trust: the code link is empty in the submitted PDF despite repeated open-source claims, Table 1 reports 'Mean ADD' values that are hard to interpret against standard BOP protocols, Figure 1's claim that FoundationPose fails under camera rotation may reflect suboptimal configuration rather than an inherent flaw, and there are typos (e.g., 'Segementation').
No limitations section is included, despite obvious limitations (synthetic occlusion simulation, single-object focus, dependency on FoundationPose quality, mask-based training).

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: fully automatic, annotation-free 6D pose estimation and tracking with failure detection and re-localization, which prior render-and-refine systems (FoundationPose, DeepIM, PoseRBPF) lack.

The proposed pipeline is complete and end-to-end: 3D model → rendered references → LLM/CLIP semantic prompting → HSFA feature fusion → SAM2/FastSAM prompting → FoundationPose registration, with a memory-pool-based re-registration loop.

The segmentation module (SOM) reports strong numbers on the BOP benchmark suite (mean mAP 68.5 across five datasets, claimed SOTA on four of five) with competitive runtime (0.183s), and the comparison table includes a broad set of leaderboard baselines.
Useful ablations are provided (language injection, HSFA depth, DINOv2 fine-tuning), and the authors commit to releasing code and a new tracking-failure dataset, which supports reproducibility.

The idea of reformulating tracking-failure detection as a lightweight binary classification task with attention-based matching is simple and sensible, and the reported latency overhead (13ms) is attractive for real-time use.
weaknesses: The central 'label-free / self-supervised / zero-shot' claim appears internally inconsistent with the actual training procedure. Appendix C/D state the SOM was trained on combined subsets of LMO, LM, YCBV, HB, TLESS, TUDL, TYOL and RUPC using 'each query image and its corresponding mask' — i.e., supervised mask training on the very datasets (and object instances) used for evaluation on the BOP test sets. This is instance-level supervised training, not zero-shot generalization, and undermines the headline claims and Table 2's 'self-supervised' framing.

Limited and potentially circular evaluation for the main pose results (Table 1): only two baselines (FP+CNOS, FP+GT) on two datasets, no error bars or statistical significance, and on YCB-Video STORM's numbers (0.78/0.99/0.74) are identical to the ground-truth-mask upper bound, which is suspicious and unexplained. The claimed 'exceeds state SOTA' is not supported against the strongest published annotation-free or model-based pose systems.

The tracking evaluation (Table 3, Q3) relies on synthetically modified YCB-Video (randomly dropped frames, randomly overlaid masks to simulate occlusion), which does not convincingly demonstrate robustness to real occlusion, rapid motion, or viewpoint exits; the protocol for computing 'Mean recall (ADD, ADD-S, AR)' for TOM vs FP Tracking is underspecified.

The technical novelty is modest relative to the framing: HSFA is standard self-/cross-attention with AdaNorm-Zero (borrowed from diffusion architectures) applied to DINOv2 features; the 'novel loss' is a weighted sum of existing Tversky and Focal losses; the rest is assembly of existing components (DINOv2, CLIP, gemma, FastSAM/SAM2, FoundationPose). No analysis is given of why or when HSFA helps beyond ablation curves.

Significant internal inconsistencies between main text and appendix undermine soundness and reproducibility: the Tversky parameters are α=0.3/β=0.7 in Eq. (3) but α=0.5/β=0.5 in Appendix D; the focal weight is λf=0.2 in the main text but wFocal=20.0 in the appendix (with additional Dice/IoU losses appearing only in the appendix); the SOM optimizer is AdamW in the main text but SGD in Appendix D; ADD/ADD-S are defined as distances (lower is better) in Appendix B while Table 1 reports them as higher-is-better scores. Also key architectural parameters (number of fusion iterations n, number of reference views m at inference, thresholds for failure detection) are never specified.

The 'real-time' claim is not well supported: 0.183s/image for SOM alone (~5.5 FPS), 0.265s with language injection, plus LLM description generation, FoundationPose registration, and TOM overhead; total end-to-end throughput is never reported.

Metrics and baselines in Table 2 raise questions: 'ZebraPoseSAT–EffNetB4' (ZebraPose is a pose-estimation method) is used as a supervised segmentation baseline; most unsupervised baselines are leaderboard executables without peer-reviewed descriptions; and given the training-set overlap noted above, the self-supervised vs supervised/unsupervised categorization is misleading.

Presentation issues: multiple typos ('Segementation', 'Tracking recoverd', 'state SOTA performances', 'Object Segementation'), a 'Code:' link that is empty, vague figure descriptions (Figure 5/7 plots are illegible), and hyperbolic language ('exceed state SOTA performances in an annotation-free manner') that is not matched by the evidence.

The TOM ablation (Table 4) compares only against cosine similarity on the authors' own synthetic classification dataset; no comparison to established visual re-identification or tracking-verification methods, and no evaluation of false-recovery rate (re-registering on a distractor object), which is the practically dangerous failure mode.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical and well-motivated problem: annotation-free 6D pose estimation and tracking with automatic failure detection and recovery. The re-registration mechanism (TOM) for detecting tracking loss and recovering from occlusion/rapid motion is a useful system-level contribution that most render-and-refine trackers (e.g., FoundationPose, DeepIM, PoseRBPF) lack.

The segmentation module (SOM) is evaluated comprehensively on five BOP core datasets against a broad set of supervised and unsupervised baselines (Table 2), and reports competitive or better mean mAP (68.5) than the strongest supervised method (67.5) with reasonable runtime.

The paper is organized around clear research questions (Q1–Q4), and each is answered with both quantitative tables and qualitative visualizations. Ablations on HSFA depth, language injection, DINOv2 fine-tuning, and the attention-based tracking classifier (Tables 4–6) support the main design choices.
The proposed system is claimed to be open-source, and a new tracking-failure dataset (200k pairs) is introduced, which is potentially useful for future work.
The writing is generally clear, and the appendix provides algorithmic detail (HSFA pseudocode), metric definitions, and training/implementation details that aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: Internal inconsistencies in the supervision claims undermine the 'label-free' narrative. The main text states that SOM training uses no class labels or pose annotations, yet Appendix D explicitly describes training 'each query image and its corresponding mask' from BOP subsets — masks are annotations. The paper also trains on training splits of the very datasets it evaluates on (LM-O, YCB-V, T-LESS, etc.), which weakens the zero-shot/self-supervised generalization claims relative to unsupervised leaderboard baselines. This needs clarification and honest reframing.

The pose estimation comparison (Table 1) is narrow: STORM is essentially FoundationPose with SOM masks vs. FoundationPose with CNOS masks, plus an upper-bound with ground-truth masks. Notably, STORM's YCB-Video numbers (0.78/0.99/0.74) are identical to the FP+Ground Truth row, which is surprising and insufficiently explained. No comparison against other recent pipelines (e.g., SAM-6D end-to-end, or FoundationPose with other segmentation front-ends) is provided, so the claim of 'exceeding SOTA' is only weakly supported for pose estimation.

The TOM evaluation relies on a synthetically modified YCB-V (randomly dropped frames, random masks over object regions), and the negative training samples are generated in a very similar way (shifted crops, random regions, distractors). This makes the failure-detection evaluation somewhat circular; performance on real occlusions, real rapid motion, and genuine object disappearance is not convincingly demonstrated beyond a single qualitative example (Figure 4).

Novelty is modest: the system assembles established components (DINOv2, SAM2/FastSAM, CLIP, an LLM, FoundationPose). The core technical additions — a hierarchical cross-attention fusion block (HSFA) and a lightweight binary classifier for tracking verification — are competent but incremental, and the loss formulation (Tversky + focal) is standard.

The 'real-time' claim is strained. SOM alone averages 0.183 s/image (0.265 s with language prompting per Table 5), plus tracking, classifier, and per-frame verification overhead; the paper never reports the end-to-end per-frame latency of the full STORM pipeline.

Hyperparameter and setup inconsistencies between the main text and appendix (e.g., AdamW with 80,000 steps and Tversky α=0.3/β=0.7 in the main text vs. SGD and Tversky α=0.5/β=0.5 with w_Tversky=0.2 in Appendix D; 'three-layer HSFA' vs. the 3/7-layer ablation) create confusion about the actual configuration. Metrics are also reported inconsistently (fractions in Table 1, percentages in Table 3).

Several presentation issues reduce polish: typos ('Segementation', 'recoverd', 'TYOL'), the code link in the abstract appears empty, and the claim that SOM surpasses 'state-of-the-art supervised baselines' partly rests on leaderboard entries without peer-reviewed publications.

The paper lacks a dedicated limitations discussion (e.g., behavior on symmetric or textureless objects, dependence on the quality of the 3D model and LLM description, multi-object association limits), which the authors are well positioned to provide given the system's dependence on many heuristics (similarity thresholds, memory pool management).

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple research questions: segmentation quality on five BOP datasets (Table 2), pose accuracy vs. CNOS baseline and GT-mask oracle (Table 1), SAM3D geometry impact (Table 3), and tracking failure detection/recovery (Tables 4-5), with multi-seed variance reporting for their own results.

The proposed SOM achieves 67.7 mAP with a single reference view, outperforming strong annotation-free baselines (NOCTIS, SAM6D, CNOS) and the best supervised baseline (ZebraPoseSAT, 67.5) on BOP segmentation, at competitive latency (0.046s), which is a practically meaningful result.

The tracking-failure verification idea (TOM) is well-motivated and the temporal policy is ablated convincingly: Table 9 shows the EMA+L rule reduces false re-localization from ~80-89% to ~2-3% under transient noise, and Table 5 shows learned attention-based matching substantially beats cosine similarity (98.36% vs 87.55% accuracy).
The closed-loop recovery claim is supported both quantitatively (Table 4: large gains over FP Tracking without failure detection) and qualitatively (Figure 4).

Detailed reproducibility material: full training/augmentation hyperparameters, runtime profiling per component (Table 6), threshold calibration procedure, and stress-test construction (Appendices C-H).

Honest limitations section that clarifies the 'zero-shot' terminology (annotation-free/adaptation-free inference, not category-disjoint generalization), acknowledges dependence on FoundationPose and SAM3D quality, and notes TOM's fixed threshold as a deployment concern.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty of the core components. HSFA is a composition of standard self-attention, cross-attention, and FiLM/AdaLN conditioning (Algorithm 1), and the 'energy-like score' is simply the negated BCE logit (E = -g_theta), which the authors themselves concede is only an inference-time renaming. Both modules are sensible engineering but incremental relative to existing reference-conditioned segmentation and OOD-style scoring.

Evaluation fairness concerns in the headline segmentation result (Table 2). STORM is trained on the training splits of the very datasets it is evaluated on (LM, LMO, T-LESS, TUD-L, HB, YCB-V plus SA-V/RUAPC), i.e., fully supervised training with masks; the 'annotation/adaptation-free' framing versus supervised baselines that are 'fine-tuned per object category' obscures that both regimes use benchmark-derived supervision. The claimed advantage is at inference time only, and the table caption risks overstating the distinction.

TOM's verification results (Table 5) are evaluated on the synthetic verification dataset whose negatives were constructed by the authors, and the TOM training data (Appendix H.3) derives from the same BOP objects used in the stress test (YCB-V, whose training split is also in SOM's training set), so the 98% accuracy and the Table 4 gains may overestimate generalization to genuinely unseen objects; no cross-dataset or category-disjoint TOM evaluation is provided.

The stress test is synthetic (random frame dropping and zero-filled rectangles with p=0.1, Appendix H.4) rather than real fast motion/occlusion, so the recovery claims in the abstract about 'severe occlusions and rapid viewpoint changes' rest on a relatively mild, artificially constructed perturbation regime plus one qualitative example.

Baseline coverage for the tracking comparison is thin: Table 1 compares only against FP+CNOS and a GT-mask oracle, and Table 4 only against 'FP Tracking' without failure detection; no comparison to other recent trackers or to simpler drift-detection heuristics that could isolate the contribution of TOM versus the mask quality of SOM.

Internal inconsistencies and unclear reporting: Table 8 reports AP of 44.0/94.6/95.4% for HSFA ablations, which is inconsistent in scale with the 67.7 mAP of Table 2 and unexplained; Figure 1 and Figure 4 rest on single cherry-picked FoundationPose failure examples; Table 2 reports variance only for STORM because 'second-order metrics were not available for the baselines'; and the code footnote is empty ('Code available at .').

The RQ1 claim that STORM 'matches the ground-truth setup exactly' on YCB-Video is imprecise (77.0 vs 78.0 ADD-AUC), and the SAM3D alignment analysis (Table 3) relies on aligning reconstructed meshes to the benchmark CAD models, which the authors admit is only for benchmark reporting - leaving deployment-relevant accuracy of unaligned single-image reconstruction essentially unquantified (22.2 VSD unaligned).

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation covering multiple aspects of the pipeline: annotation-free pose estimation (LM-O, YCB-V), BOP instance segmentation across 5 datasets with comparisons to leaderboard systems, SAM3D reconstruction quality, failure-detection ablations, and detailed runtime profiling (Tables 2, 6, 7)

The SOM segmentation results are genuinely strong: 67.7 mean AP with a single reference view, outperforming annotation-free baselines and rivaling the strongest supervised, per-category fine-tuned method, at competitive latency

Honest and unusually thorough limitations section that explicitly disambiguates 'zero-shot' as annotation-free/adaptation-free rather than category-disjoint generalization, and acknowledges dependence on SAM3D/FoundationPose quality, symmetric/textureless object failure modes, and fixed threshold calibration

Well-documented implementation details in the appendix (augmentation, loss weights, optimizer settings, threshold calibration procedure, state-machine policy), and a sensible temporal policy (EMA + L-consecutive frames) that is ablated against naive per-frame triggering (Table 9)
The tracking-failure detection framing is practically useful: explicit verification of tracking validity with automatic re-initialization addresses a real, underexplored gap in current pose trackers
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: HSFA is a composition of standard components (self-attention, cross-attention, FiLM/AdaLN conditioning, iterative refinement), and TOM is a BCE-trained binary verifier whose 'energy-like score' is simply the negated logit — the paper itself concedes (Sec 3.2.2) that no energy-model training is involved, making the energy framing largely cosmetic. Much of the system is an integration of frozen foundation models (DINOv3, SAM3D, FoundationPose, CLIP/Gemma, SAM2), so the contribution is closer to systems engineering than a new learning principle

Internal inconsistencies undermine confidence in the evaluation: Table 8 reports 94.6/95.4 AP for HSFA3/HSFA7 ablations, while the main Table 2 reports 67.7 mean AP — the protocol or test set for the ablation is unclear and unexplained. ADD_AUC values also differ between Table 1 (74.0) and Table 4 (74.64) without reconciliation. Text claims 'exceeds the strong CNOS baseline by 5%' on YCB-V when the delta is 4 points

The headline failure-detection/recovery evaluation (RQ4, Table 4) relies on synthetic corruptions — random frame dropping and random rectangular masks placed using ground-truth object masks — which are weak proxies for real occlusion and fast motion, and the TOM verification metrics (Table 5) are computed on synthetically generated negatives (distractor swaps, random crops) that are likely much easier than genuine drift; AUROC is only 96.4% despite 98.4% accuracy, suggesting hard failures remain unresolved

The SAM3D 'model-free' claim is weakened by the alignment procedure: Table 3 shows SAM3D+FP collapses without alignment (ADD-S 44.92) but matches GT+FP with alignment (99.12), and that alignment uses ICP against the ground-truth benchmark CAD mesh. The argument that deployment needs only a self-consistent frame is plausible but the evaluated pose numbers are not achievable without GT-CAD-derived scale/pose alignment, which is arguably a form of test-time ground-truth usage

Comparisons for the pose-estimation results (RQ1) are narrow: only FP+CNOS and the FP+GT oracle, with no comparison to other recent annotation-free pose pipelines (e.g., SAM-6D end-to-end, Pos3R), and Figure 1 rests on a single cherry-picked FoundationPose failure despite FoundationPose's documented robustness

Presentation and completeness issues: the code URL and conflict-of-interest disclosure are empty placeholders; typos ('This design gives SOM a learned alternative' in the HSFA section, 'Tracking recoverd' in Figure 4); the claimed 'Tracking Failure Benchmark' contribution is in fact synthetic corruptions of YCB-V rather than a new benchmark with real failure data; and the paper reads more as a CVPR/robotics systems paper than a fit for ICML's methodological scope

strengths: Comprehensive evaluation decomposed into five explicit research questions (RQ1–RQ5), covering end-to-end pose estimation, segmentation, 3D reconstruction quality, and tracking failure detection, with both quantitative tables and runtime profiling.

Strong empirical results: SOM achieves the best mean AP (67.7) among annotation-free methods across five BOP datasets, surpassing even per-category supervised baselines, and STORM closes most of the gap to the ground-truth-mask upper bound in Table 1.

The tracking-loss verification idea (TOM) addresses a genuine, well-motivated gap: existing trackers like FoundationPose drift silently and lack a built-in validity signal. The temporal EMA + L-consecutive-frame policy is shown to reduce false re-localization from ~80-89% to ~2-3% (Table 9), which is a convincing diagnostic.

The paper is notably honest in several places: it clarifies that 'energy' is only an inference-time transformation of a BCE logit rather than an energy-based training objective, that 'zero-shot' means annotation-free/adaptation-free rather than category-disjoint generalization, and the limitations section candidly discusses reliance on SAM3D/FoundationPose fidelity, symmetric/textureless object ambiguity, and static thresholds.

Good reproducibility detail in appendices: training data splits, augmentation, loss weights, hyperparameters (EMA α=0.9, L=3, K=16), threshold calibration procedure, and hardware/runtime profiles are all documented.

Well-structured writing with clear framing of the reference-query distributional shift problem, and informative ablations (HSFA depth, reference count k, language conditioning, attention depth in TOM).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the trainable components are a fairly standard composition of self-attention, cross-attention, AdaLN/FiLM conditioning (HSFA) and a BCE-trained crop-pair classifier (TOM). The system's strength derives largely from frozen foundation models (DINOv3, CLIP/VLM, SAM3D, FoundationPose), making this more of a strong systems/engineering contribution than a new learning principle.

The claimed 'Tracking Failure Benchmark' contribution is weaker than advertised: it is primarily synthetic corruptions of YCB-Video (frame dropping with p=0.1 and random rectangular occlusions with p=0.1), which may not reflect realistic drift and occlusion statistics. The tracking-recovery comparison (Table 4) is only against the authors' own pipeline without TOM and against FoundationPose alone; no external tracker with re-detection capability (e.g., FoundationPose re-initialized by CNOS-style detection, MegaPose-based loops) is compared.
No working code link: footnote 1 reads 'Code available at .' with an empty URL, which materially harms reproducibility for a system paper whose contribution is largely the integration itself.

Inconsistency in reported numbers: Table 1 reports STORM ADD/ADD-S/AR of 74.0/89.0/53.0 on LM-O while Table 4 reports 74.64/88.56/67.85 for the same-named method; the differing protocols are not clearly reconciled, and the AR jump of ~15 points between tables is unexplained.

The headline Table 1 gains partly rest on replacing CNOS masks with SOM masks in a fixed FoundationPose pipeline; it is not always clear how much of the improvement is attributable to the proposed HSFA architecture versus simply a better segmentation model (or better training data mixture with SA-V/RUAPC).

The RQ3 evaluation uses ICP alignment of SAM3D meshes to the ground-truth CAD models for benchmark reporting; while the paper honestly notes this is benchmark-convention only, it weakens the 'no CAD required' deployment narrative and the unaligned setting performs drastically worse (VSD 22.19 vs 60.72).

Some claims are under-supported by baselines: Table 5 shows the learned verifier improves over cosine similarity by only ~2 AUROC points, and TOM gains are evaluated only on the authors' synthetic dataset; there is no external validation of the failure-detection AUROC/accuracy on real occlusion events.

Minor presentation defects: Figure 2 references 'SOM' inconsistently ('This design gives SOM...'), Figure 4 contains a typo ('Tracking recoverd'), the Frame 1 anecdote rests on a single qualitative FoundationPose failure, and the ± std in Table 1 over '5 independent runs' is not explained given an otherwise largely deterministic pipeline.

Training data overlap concern: SOM is trained on BOP training splits of the same datasets used in Table 2 evaluation (LM, LM-O, T-LESS, TUD-L, HB, YCB-V) plus renders from object models; although test scenes are excluded and this is disclosed, calling the supervised baselines 'fine-tuned per object category' while SOM is trained on the same benchmark domains softens the claimed advantage.
